def test_moving_a_rest_catalog_uri_asks_for_the_primary_token(db_session: Any) -> None:
    """The review-caught hole in the first cut of this guard, and the reason
    `catalog_uri` is listed under BOTH slots.

    `catalog_properties` puts both credentials at that one address: the catalog
    password is injected into `props["uri"]`, and `props[secret_property] = secret`
    is sent TO that uri — for a REST catalog `secret_property` is `token`, which
    pyiceberg presents as `Authorization: Bearer …`.

    So on the commonest REST shape — a `secret_ref` and NO `catalog_secret_name` —
    listing `catalog_uri` under the `catalog` slot alone waved the move straight
    through: the catalog slot found nothing stored and skipped, and the `secret`
    slot's other fields hadn't moved. Every other test here reaches `catalog_uri`
    through the catalog slot, which is exactly why none of them saw it.
    """
    store = FakeSecretStore()
    conn = svc.create_connection(
        db_session,
        name="rest-iceberg",
        conn_type="iceberg",
        env="dev",
        config={
            "catalog_type": "rest",
            "catalog_uri": "https://catalog.internal",
            "secret_property": "token",
        },
        secret="the-bearer-token",
        created_by=_user(db_session).id,
        secret_store=store,
    )
    assert conn.config.get("catalog_secret_name") is None

    with pytest.raises(svc.CredentialRedirectError) as exc:
        svc.update_connection(
            db_session,
            conn.id,
            config={
                "catalog_type": "rest",
                "catalog_uri": "https://attacker.example.com",
                "secret_property": "token",
            },
            secret_store=store,
        )

    assert exc.value.detail["required"] == ["secret"]
    assert conn.config["catalog_uri"] == "https://catalog.internal"

# `None` is the "not supplied" signal on every credential field below, so an
# EMPTY STRING is never a meaningful value — and it is actively harmful: the
# service writes whatever it is handed straight to the SecretStore, so `""`
# replaces a working credential with a blank one and returns 200. The connection
# then has no visible state until a run fails (the #954 blindness). `reauth` has
# carried `min_length=1` since it shipped; create/update did not, which also gave
# #1401's redirect guard a hole — supplying `""` satisfied "you re-supplied the
# credential" while destroying it. Caught in the #1403 review.
_WRITE_ONLY_SECRET = {"min_length": 1}


class ConnectionCreate(ApiModel):
    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=128)
    type: str
    env: str
    config: dict[str, Any] = Field(default_factory=dict)
    secret: str | None = Field(
        default=None, description="Credential; write-only, never returned", **_WRITE_ONLY_SECRET
    )
    catalog_secret: str | None = Field(
        default=None,
        description=(
            "Second credential a connection type may need (currently the Iceberg "
            "SQL-catalog DB password, #1181); write-only, never returned"
        ),
        **_WRITE_ONLY_SECRET,
    )

    secret: str | None = Field(

    )
    catalog_secret: str | None = Field(
        default=None,
        description="Rotate the second (catalog) credential; write-only",
        **_WRITE_ONLY_SECRET,

# `None` is the "not supplied" signal on every credential field below, so an
# EMPTY STRING is never a meaningful value — and it is actively harmful: the
# service writes whatever it is handed straight to the SecretStore, so `""`
# replaces a working credential with a blank one and returns 200. The connection
# then has no visible state until a run fails (the #954 blindness). `reauth` has
# carried `min_length=1` since it shipped; create/update did not, which also gave

# credential" while destroying it. Caught in the #1403 review.

1	"""Connection CRUD + connectivity-test endpoints.
2	
3	Thin HTTP layer over `connection_service`: validates request shapes, wires the
4	current user + db session + secret store, and maps models onto responses. All
5	business logic (validation dispatch, secret write-through, connectivity probe)
6	lives in the service. Responses never carry secret material — only `has_secret`.
7	
8	Both `/test` routes (the saved-connection `/connections/{id}/test` and the
9	draft `/connections/test`, #351) are sync ``def`` so FastAPI runs them in a
10	worker thread; the datasource connect is blocking and must not stall the
11	event loop.
12	
13	## Authorization (ADR 0033 / #741) — connections are the one workspace-global resource
14	
15	Connections are **shared infrastructure holding credentials**: they are not
16	owned, not shared per-user, and every suite in the workspace runs on them. That
17	is why the role gates here are the sharpest in the app, and why they are
18	per-route rather than declared once on the router:
19	
20	    create / update / delete / reauth   AdminUser   — mutating shared credentialed infra
21	    test (draft, unsaved)               AdminUser   — probes CALLER-SUPPLIED config
22	    test (saved)                        MemberUser  — Members verify, Viewers do not probe
23	    list / get / versions               any authenticated user
24	
25	The two `test` routes deliberately differ, and the split is about *whose config
26	is being probed* rather than who is asking — see `test_draft_connection`.
27	
28	The read routes keeping the plain `get_current_user` is a **decision, not an
29	omission**: a Member authoring a suite must be able to see and reference the
30	connections available to them. No tier has ever been able to read a credential
31	back out — responses carry `has_secret`, never secret material — so widening
32	reads costs nothing that the Admin gate is protecting.

# ───────────────────────── create ──────────────────────────────────


def test_create_returns_201_and_hides_secret(
    client: tuple[TestClient, FakeSecretStore], db_session: Any
) -> None:
    api, store = client
    resp = api.post("/api/v1/connections", json=_create_payload())

    assert resp.status_code == 201
    body = resp.json()
    assert body["type"] == "snowflake"
    assert body["has_secret"] is True
    # secret material must never appear in the response
    assert "secret" not in body
    assert "secret_ref" not in body
    # persisted + written through to the store
    conn = db_session.get(Connection, uuid.UUID(body["id"]))
    assert conn is not None
    assert store.data[conn.secret_ref] == "p@ss"


def test_create_unknown_type_returns_422(client: tuple[TestClient, FakeSecretStore]) -> None:
    api, _ = client

- Datasource credentials, webhook signing keys, and channel secrets are held in a **secret
  store behind a seam** — Azure Key Vault in the primary reference deployment, AWS Secrets

725:| ✅ | [#1118](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1118) **`*_secret_name` SSRF / credential-exfiltration closed** — the class W5 deferred to this track. `*_secret_name` keys were already *documented* as server-owned bookkeeping and enforced nowhere, which made them an exfiltration primitive: read a victim connection's ref off the (deliberately workspace-global) `GET /connections`, create or draft-test an `iceberg` connection carrying that ref plus a `catalog_uri` you control, and the server resolves the real credential and posts it to you. ADR 0033's gates narrowed *who* could reach the entry points but did not close it — an Admin who may **rotate** a credential still may not **read** it, and this turned the first power into the second. The mitigation is **round-trip fidelity, not a ban**: a caller may echo back a `*_secret_name` byte-identical to the one already stored on that connection (so the GET → edit-one-field → PATCH-whole-config flow still works) but can never introduce or repoint one; create and the trace-less draft test have no stored row to compare against, so any `*_secret_name` is foreign by definition and the draft path no longer resolves them at all. Raises 422 rather than silently stripping, because a request whose meaning is quietly altered is how someone ends up debugging a connection that "lost" its catalog credential. All three attack paths (create, update-repoint, draft-test) are mutation-verified against the pre-fix code. fixup: close the review-caught REST-catalog hole, the blank-secret bypass, and the edit-open flash

Four findings from the /code-review, all real:

   was listed under the `catalog` slot only, but `catalog_properties` puts BOTH
   credentials at that address: the catalog password is injected into `props["uri"]`
   and `props[secret_property] = secret` is sent TO that uri — for a REST catalog
   `secret_property` is `token`, which pyiceberg presents as a bearer. On the
   commonest REST shape (a `secret_ref`, no `catalog_secret_name`) the catalog slot
   found nothing stored and waved the move through while the primary token followed
   the URI. `catalog_uri` now sits in both slots, frontend mirrored, with the REST
   case as a test — every prior test reached `catalog_uri` through the catalog slot,
   which is exactly why none of them saw it.

2. An empty-string secret satisfied "you re-supplied the credential" while blanking
   it — a quiet destroy-and-move. Pre-existing on main: `reauth` has carried
   `min_length=1` since it shipped, create/update never did, so `PATCH {"secret": ""}`
   bricks a credential today and the connection has no visible state until a run
   fails (#954). Bounded on both write models.

   `Form.useWatch` returns undefined before the seeding effect runs — so the warning

   asserting something untrue of the current state. The comparison moved into a pure
   `movedDestinationFields`, where "not yet known" means nothing moved and the case is
   unit-testable; RTL only ever observes the settled post-effect DOM.

| GET | `/me/api-keys` | List your keys (metadata only, never the token). |
| DELETE | `/me/api-keys/{id}` | Revoke a key. |

| POST | `/connections/{id}/test` | Test live connectivity. |

## 1. Connect a datasource

1. Go to **Connections → Add connection**.
2. Pick your datasource type (Snowflake, Unity Catalog, ADLS Gen2, S3, or Apache
   Iceberg). The form is spec-driven — it asks only for what that type needs.
3. Fill it in with a **read-only** credential (for Snowflake, key-pair auth is recommended),
   then click **Test**. A green result means DataQ can reach it.

*Tip:* name it for its environment — e.g. `snowflake-prod` — so a suite's env is unambiguous.

## 2. Create a suite and point it at a target

=== orchestration 40-52 ===
with no host API dependency (ADR 0029). dbt Core has no callback hook like Airflow's, so
you run a tiny **post-build wrapper**:

- Register a **dbt connection** (Connections → dbt) with its `project_name`, the `jobs` it
  publishes, and the `artifacts_uri` where builds land (`adls://…`, `s3://…`, or `file://…`)
  plus the store's read credential.
  > **`artifacts_uri` is the base prefix, not the full published path** — DataQ appends
  > `/<job>/latest/…` itself. If your publisher writes
  > `adls://<account>/<container>/<prefix>/dbt/latest/run_results.json`, register
  > `artifacts_uri: adls://<account>/<container>/<prefix>` with `jobs: ["dbt"]`. Pasting the
  > publisher's own output variable verbatim usually double-counts the job segment (the poll
  > then looks in `<prefix>/dbt/dbt/latest/` and finds nothing).
- Copy the callback snippet
=== recommended 105,122 ===
workspace-wide reach), set a sensible expiry, and rotate it like any credential. The assistant
acts **as that user** — it sees exactly what the user can.

## 8. Set up access

**Do:** users sign in via **SSO**. Add workspace admins via the `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS`
allowlist; share individual suites (**view / edit**) from the suite.

**Recommended:**

- **Share by default with `view`**; reserve `edit` for the owning team.
- **Keep `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS` minimal** — a workspace admin can read *every* suite's
  results, including failing-row samples (the one place PII lands), and manage/delete any
  suite (ADR 0027). For a regulated/PHI deployment, treat the access-audit trail as a
  prerequisite before granting it broadly.

# Post-v1 notes — Admin, access model & UI/IA (deferred design)

> **Status: deferred to post-v1.** Captured so the design intent isn't lost. We
> intentionally did **not** build the admin/IAM console in v1. For a single-tenant
> tool used by one trusted data team, a full RBAC console (admin write console,
> user-disable, per-connection ownership restrictions, an access matrix) is
> gold-plating. The market-leading DQ tools (Great Expectations, Soda, dbt tests,
> Monte Carlo) lead with **checks → results → trends → alerts**, not user-lifecycle
> management. v1 ships suite-level sharing + a read-only admin view; everything
> else is recorded here for later.

> actions), both milestoned _v1.1 Backlog_ (the milestone formerly named _Backlog (post-v1 / testing)_).

  axis, **no** Azure/Entra claim read in route/service code, no migration. `dataq-admin`
  is the workspace-admin.

### Moving a connection to a new host

Editing a field that decides *where* the credential is sent — Snowflake `account`, ADLS
`account_url`, S3/dbt `endpoint_url`, Unity Catalog `workspace_url`, Iceberg `catalog_uri` /
`warehouse` / `properties`, Airflow `base_url`, dbt `artifacts_uri` — requires re-entering
that credential in the same save. The edit form asks for it as soon as you change one of
those fields; through the API the request is rejected with `422 credential_redirect` until
you include it.

This is deliberate. A stored credential is never forwarded to a destination the caller
changed, so an Admin who may *rotate* a credential still cannot *read* one by pointing the
connection at a host they control and pressing Test. Moving a connection is fully supported —
doing it with a credential you don't know is not.""")

docs: reconcile the published docs with workspace roles (ADR 0033) and the credential-redirect guard

An audit of `docs/` found 15 statements the RBAC track (#1396–#1400) and the
credential-redirect fix (#1403) made wrong, incomplete, or actively misleading.
Both shipped in the same session; neither swept the wider doc set.

The ones that would have cost a reader real time:

- `architecture.md` — the `users` ERD had no `role` column, and the shares note
  still described workspace-admin as "a config allowlist, not a share row". That
  allowlist is now a bootstrap seed and break-glass that only ever grants.
- `api-keys.md` — the load-bearing claim ("a PAT inherits exactly your per-suite
  access; if you can see a suite, your key can") is now false for connections: a
  Member's PAT gets 403 on `POST /connections` regardless of any suite grant. A
  PAT inherits BOTH axes, and both resolve per request.
- `tutorial.md` and `orchestration.md` — walkthroughs that open by telling every
  reader to go create a connection, which is Admin-only. A Member following the
  tutorial verbatim fills in a credential form and then hits the gate.
- `recommended-usage.md` §8 — instructed operators to grant admin by editing
  `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS`, which is no longer the mechanism.
- `rest-api.md` — `/me` returns `role`, connection routes have per-role gates, and
  `credential_redirect` is a 422 an operator will meet during a host migration.
  None of it was documented.

Also adds the operator-facing half of #1403 (`datasources-checks.md` "Moving a
connection to a new host", plus troubleshooting entries for the 422 and the 403),
strikes through the two lines in ADR 0027 that its own 0033 amendment says are
stale but never edited, and banners `post-v1-admin-ui-notes.md`, whose "a full
RBAC console is gold-plating for a single-tenant tool" decision is contradicted
by what shipped — the single-tenant premise was the problem, not the mitigation.
